seo.title: 27 Famous Mascot Logos Explained
seo.description: 27 famous mascot logos explained by a brand designer: people, animals and made-up characters from KFC, Quaker and Pringles to Mailchimp, Duolingo and the Michelin Man.

description: 27 famous mascot logos explained by a brand designer: people, animals and made-up characters from KFC, Quaker and Pringles to Mailchimp, Duolingo and the Michelin Man.
intro:
A mascot logo puts a character at the heart of the logo: a person, an animal or a made-up creature with a face and a personality. Colonel Sanders on KFC, the Michelin Man and the Duolingo owl are all mascot logos. A mascot gives a brand someone to recognise, remember and like, which is why these characters often outlive the people who drew them.

Logo design quick course: this guide is part of my series on logo types. Read the others on combination marks, emblem logos, script logos, wordmark logos, monogram logos, lettermark logos, abstract logos, symmetry and negative space, or start with the overview of all types of logos.

What is a mascot logo?

A mascot logo is a logo built around a character. It is usually a combination mark: the character sits next to, above or inside the brand name. KFC, Quaker and Mailchimp work this way. Some mascots are so famous that they work alone, like the Starbucks siren or the GitHub Octocat.

Not every brand mascot is a mascot logo. The Geico gecko, the Energizer Bunny and Tony the Tiger are famous characters, but they live in ads and on packs, not in the logo itself. This article only covers mascots that are part of the logo.

Where mascot logos come from

Mascot logos grew up with packaged food. In the late 1800s, shoppers stopped scooping oats, salt and crackers out of barrels and started buying sealed, branded packs. A friendly face on the box helped people pick the same product again. Quaker registered its man in Quaker clothes in 1877, the first trademark for a breakfast cereal.

Posters made the next generation of mascots famous. The French artist O'Galop drew Bibendum, the Michelin Man, in 1898, raising a glass full of nails and broken glass: a tyre that "drinks up obstacles". In 1916, a schoolboy named Antonio Gentile sent Planters a sketch of a peanut with arms and legs, and Mr. Peanut was born.

Three types of mascot logos

People: KFC, Quaker, Gerber and Sun-Maid put a human face on the brand. Some are real people, like Colonel Sanders. Others were invented to stand for an idea, like honesty for Quaker or home cooking for Big Boy.

Animals: Mailchimp, Duolingo, Aflac and WWF use an animal with a clear personality. Animals are easy to draw, easy to like and work in any country.

Made-up characters: Mr. Peanut, the Michelin Man, Reddit's alien and GitHub's Octocat don't exist in nature. Made-up characters are the easiest to own, because no one else can use the same creature.

Why tech startups love mascots

Mascots aren't only for cereal boxes. Mailchimp, Duolingo, GitHub, Reddit, Docker, Android and Waze all use characters. In a crowded software market, where many logos are blue shapes and clean sans serif type, a character is the fastest way to look different. It also gives the product a voice: Duo the owl's pushy reminders turned Duolingo into a meme.

The problem with mascot logos: detail and age

Mascots are harder to shrink than most logos. A detailed portrait like the Quaker man looks great on a canister and turns to mush on a favicon. A mascot drawn from a few bold shapes, like the WWF panda, still reads at 16 pixels.

That is why so many mascots get simpler over time. Quaker slimmed its man down in 2012, Mailchimp turned Freddie into a one-colour silhouette in 2018 and Pringles removed Mr. P's hair in 2020. Some mascots don't survive at all. Land O'Lakes removed Mia from its packaging in 2020, and the Aunt Jemima and Uncle Ben's characters were dropped in 2020 and 2021 after years of criticism that they were based on racial stereotypes. A mascot is a person in your brand, so it has to age well.

How I made my own mascot

In graphic design school, I designed my own brand mascot as a personal project. It went all the way to a physical product: a plush character in a clear box, with packaging and a little brochure inside.

From the first sketches to the final illustrations, I wanted a character that was unique and memorable, with a personality people would get straight away. Ebaq is a blue letter e with big eyes and a tongue sticking out.

As you may notice, Ebaq borrows parts from Mickey Mouse. Yes! I took a plush toy, removed the hands and feet, and used them to build my own mascot. He stands for the playful, adventurous side of my brand, and the project taught me the most important rule of mascots: give the character one clear personality.

Below are 27 famous mascot logos, American brands first and then the rest of the world, across fast food, packaged food, tech, insurance, retail and charity. Each one has a slide with my handwritten notes and a short explanation.

logoResearch.name: KFC
logoResearch.verifiedFact: KFC's first logo put Colonel Harland Sanders' face on the sign in 1952, and a 2026 redesign by JKR turned the bucket stripes into the letters K, F and C.
observations: The Colonel's face sits between red stripes that spell KFC.
A real founder's face makes the chicken feel like one man's recipe.

logoResearch.name: Quaker
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Quaker registered its man in Quaker clothes in 1877, the first trademark for a breakfast cereal, and a 2012 update made him slimmer and younger.
observations: A smiling man in a black hat and white collar sits above the word Quaker.
He was never a real person; the Quaker figure was chosen to suggest honesty.

logoResearch.name: Pringles
logoResearch.verifiedFact: JKR gave Mr. P his first redesign in more than 20 years in 2020, dropping his hair and adding bold eyebrows.
observations: A face made of eyes, eyebrows and a huge moustache.
With no mouth or nose, he is simple enough to print on any can.

logoResearch.name: Big Boy
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Bob Wian named his double-decker burger after a six-year-old customer, Richard Woodruff, in 1937, and a sketch of the boy became the mascot.
observations: A boy in checked overalls holds a burger above his head.
The checks and the quiff make him easy to spot from the road.

logoResearch.name: Morton Salt
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Morton Umbrella Girl first appeared in 1914 with the line "When it rains it pours".
observations: A girl under an umbrella spills salt behind her as she walks in the rain.
The picture shows the promise: the salt still pours when it's damp.

logoResearch.name: Gerber
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Dorothy Hope Smith drew the Gerber Baby in 1928, using a baby named Ann Turner Cook as the model.
observations: A charcoal sketch of a baby's face sits above a heavy serif wordmark.
Smith offered to finish the sketch, but Gerber liked it as it was.

logoResearch.name: Little Caesars
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Mike and Marian Ilitch opened the first Little Caesars in Garden City, Michigan, in 1959.
observations: A little Roman in a toga holds up a pizza on a spear.
The joke is in the name: a tiny Caesar selling cheap pizza.

logoResearch.name: Sun-Maid
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Lorraine Collett posed for the Sun-Maid girl in 1915, wearing a red bonnet and holding a tray of grapes.
observations: A smiling girl in a red bonnet holds a tray of grapes in front of the sun.
A real person in a sunny field tells you the raisins are dried in the sun.

logoResearch.name: Bic
logoResearch.verifiedFact: French poster artist Raymond Savignac drew the Bic Boy in 1961, with a pen ball for a head.
observations: A small boy hides a pen behind his back, next to the orange Bic box.
The ball head shows off the product's best feature: the ballpoint.

logoResearch.name: Mailchimp
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Collins redrew Freddie the chimp as a one-colour, winking silhouette in Mailchimp's 2018 rebrand.
observations: A winking chimp in a postman's hat sits next to the wordmark.
The wink makes email marketing, a dull job, feel playful.

logoResearch.name: Duolingo
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Duolingo's in-house team redrew Duo the owl in 2019 to make him easier to animate.
observations: A round green owl built from simple shapes.
Duo's pushy reminders turned the owl into a meme.

logoResearch.name: Aflac
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Aflac duck first quacked in an ad on New Year's Day 2000 and joined the logo in 2005.
observations: A white duck stands in for the l in Aflac.
The duck shouts the name in ads, so people learned to say Aflac.

logoResearch.name: Docker
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Docker's whale won a 99designs contest in 2013, and the community named it Moby Dock.
observations: A chunky black whale sits next to a lowercase wordmark.
Older versions stacked containers on the whale; the 2026 logo keeps just the whale.

logoResearch.name: Chuck E. Cheese
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Atari founder Nolan Bushnell opened the first Chuck E. Cheese in San Jose in 1977.
observations: A grinning grey mouse in a cap peeks out of a red circle.
A cartoon mouse tells kids the place is for them, not their parents.

logoResearch.name: Hush Puppies
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Wolverine launched Hush Puppies in 1958 with a photo of a basset hound, later named Jason, as the logo.
observations: A sad-eyed basset hound sits above a plain wordmark.
The droopy dog promises comfort, like a shoe for tired feet.

logoResearch.name: Tripadvisor
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Tripadvisor's owl is called Ollie, and a 2025 redesign by Koto took him out of his circle.
observations: Ollie is just two big eyes and a beak.
Owls are wise, which suits a site built on reviews.

logoResearch.name: WWF
logoResearch.verifiedFact: WWF's panda logo was drawn in 1961 from Chi-Chi, a giant panda at London Zoo.
observations: A black and white panda built from a few solid shapes.
Black and white kept printing cheap for a new charity.

logoResearch.name: Jollibee
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Tony Tan Caktiong opened the first Jollibee in Quezon City in 1978.
observations: A smiling red bee wears a white chef's hat.
A happy bee in a chef's hat makes the chain feel like a family treat.

logoResearch.name: Planters
logoResearch.verifiedFact: A schoolboy, Antonio Gentile, drew the first Mr. Peanut in 1916 for a Planters contest.
observations: A peanut in a top hat, monocle and spats.
Planters killed him off in a 2020 Super Bowl ad, then brought him back as Baby Nut.

logoResearch.name: Mr. Clean
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Commercial artist Richard Black drew Mr. Clean as a genie for the cleaner's 1958 launch.
observations: A bald man with folded arms and one earring.
He started as a genie, which is why he looks so strong and so clean.

logoResearch.name: Chiquita
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Cartoonist Dik Browne created Miss Chiquita, a banana with a fruit hat, in 1944.
observations: A woman with a fruit hat sits on a blue oval sticker.
The sticker on every banana turned a fruit into a brand.

logoResearch.name: Starbucks
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Starbucks siren came from an old woodcut of a two-tailed siren, and the 2011 logo dropped the words around her.
observations: A crowned siren with two tails sits in a green circle.
Starbucks is so well known that the siren works without the name.

logoResearch.name: Reddit
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Co-founder Alexis Ohanian drew Snoo, Reddit's alien, in 2005.
observations: A white alien head with an antenna sits on an orange-red circle.
The 2023 redesign gave Snoo a rounder, more three-dimensional face.

logoResearch.name: GitHub
logoResearch.verifiedFact: GitHub found the Octocat on iStock; designer Simon Oxley had drawn it.
observations: A cat's head with octopus tentacles, cut out of a black circle.
Half cat, half octopus: it's odd enough to stay in your head.

logoResearch.name: Android
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Designer Irina Blok created the Android robot in 2007, and Google let anyone use it.
observations: A green robot head with two antennae sits next to the wordmark.
Anyone can use the robot, which is why it turns up everywhere.

logoResearch.name: Waze
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Pentagram redrew Waze's smiling character, the Wazer, in 2020.
observations: A smiling speech bubble on two wheels.
The face makes a traffic app feel like a friend in the car.

logoResearch.name: Michelin
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Poster artist O'Galop drew Bibendum, the Michelin Man, in 1898 from a stack of tyres.
observations: A man made of white tyres stretches out over the blue wordmark.
He is white because early tyres were pale before carbon black was added.

listIntro: The boards below show all 27 mascot logos in one consistent format, grouped into people, animals and made-up characters.
Each logo is reviewed for its design decisions, not for the size or success of the company behind it.
sectionIntroductions: These logos put a human face on the brand. Some show a real founder or model, others a character invented to stand for an idea.
Animal mascots are easy to like and work in any language. The best ones have one clear personality trait, like a wink or a quack.
Made-up characters don't exist in nature, so no one else can own them. They range from a peanut in a top hat to an alien and a robot.
sectionBridge: This is a visual study of mascot logos, not a ranking of companies.
Look at how much detail each character has, how it sits with the name and how well it would read as a small icon.

Notice how the mascot would read on a pack, a sign and a phone screen.

findings.heading: A face is easy to remember
findings.text: KFC, Quaker and Gerber put a face on the pack, and people recognise faces faster than words.

findings.heading: Simple mascots last
findings.text: WWF, GitHub and Reddit use a few bold shapes, so they still read at icon size.

findings.heading: Mascots get simpler with age
findings.text: Quaker, Mailchimp and Pringles all removed detail to keep their characters working on screens.

findings.heading: Tech uses mascots to stand out
findings.text: Mailchimp, Duolingo, Docker and Waze use characters to look different in a market full of blue shapes.

findings.heading: A mascot has to age well
findings.text: Land O'Lakes, Aunt Jemima and Uncle Ben's show that a character can become a liability when attitudes change.

logoRosterConfig.checklistHeading: A practical checklist for a mascot logo
checklistItems: Does the character say something true about the brand?
Does it have one clear personality trait?
Is it built from a few bold shapes, not fine detail?
Does the head alone work as an app icon or favicon?
Will the character still feel right in 20 years?
logoRosterConfig.conclusionHtml:
How to design a mascot logo

1. Pick a character. Choose a person, an animal or a made-up creature that says something true about the brand. A duck that shouts the name works for Aflac. A chimp in a postman's hat works for an email tool.

2. Sketch a personality. Decide who the character is before you draw details. Is it cheeky, wise, strong or kind? One clear trait, like Freddie's wink or Mr. Clean's folded arms, is easier to remember than a list.

3. Simplify the shapes. Build the character from a few bold shapes and a limited palette. Remove lines until it starts to lose its personality, then put the last one back.

4. Test it small. Check the mascot at 24 pixels, in one colour and next to the name. If the face disappears, design a simplified head or icon version, the way Reddit and Duolingo use just the head of their character.

Want a mascot that people remember?

A great mascot logo gives a brand a face, a personality and a voice. It is built from simple shapes, has one clear trait and comes with a small icon version for screens. KFC, Michelin and Duolingo prove that the right character can carry a brand for decades.

faq.question: What is a mascot logo?
faq.answer: A mascot logo is a logo built around a character, such as a person, an animal or a made-up creature. Famous examples include KFC's Colonel Sanders, the Michelin Man, Mr. Peanut and the Duolingo owl.

faq.question: What is the difference between a mascot and a mascot logo?
faq.answer: A brand mascot can appear anywhere, in ads, on packs or as a costume. A mascot logo puts the character inside the logo itself. The Geico gecko is a mascot; the Aflac duck is part of the Aflac logo.

faq.question: Are mascot logos good for startups?
faq.answer: They can be. A character helps a new brand stand out, especially in crowded markets like software, food and kids' products. Keep the design simple and plan an icon version for apps and social media.

faq.question: How do you make a mascot logo work at small sizes?
faq.answer: Build the character from a few bold shapes, limit the colours and design a simplified head or icon version. Test it at 24 pixels and in one colour before you finalise it.

faq.question: How much does a mascot logo cost?
faq.answer: It depends on how much illustration you need. I design a complete brand identity, including a simple mascot mark, in one week for a flat $3,000. A full character with many poses and animations is quoted separately.
